c.tagline: Okinawa's laid-back capital, where Ryukyu castles, island cuisine, and East China Sea beaches replace mainland Japan's rush.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are plentiful, cheap, and metered - usually the practical choice, since ride-hailing apps barely operate in Okinawa. GO and DiDi have only limited taxi-dispatch coverage in Naha; otherwise flag one on the street or wait at a rank.

emergency.note: 110 reaches the police and 119 reaches fire and ambulance, nationwide.

avoid.reason: Ignore bar touts on Kokusai-dori and in the Matsuyama nightlife district late at night to avoid inflated-bill scams.

hood_desc: The mile-long 'International Street' and the covered Makishi Public Market form the city's lively heart - souvenir shops, izakayas, Okinawan restaurants, and hotels; the obvious walkable base for first-timers.
The former royal capital on the hills east of downtown, centered on the reconstructed Shuri Castle, stone-paved lanes, and sacred Ryukyu sites; quieter and steeped in history.
A modern 'new downtown' of shopping malls, the Okinawa Prefectural Museum, duty-free shops, and upscale hotels built on former US military land; polished and easy to reach by monorail.
The seaside pocket around Naminoue Shrine and Naha's only city beach, plus the old Wakasa port district; relaxed and close to the center.
Naha's historic pottery quarter of narrow lanes, working kilns, ceramic studios, and cafes just off the Makishi market; arty and atmospheric.
lodging: Hotel Aqua Citta Naha by WBF

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though some prefer bottled for taste.

transit.pay: Tap a contactless IC card (national Suica/ICOCA or the local OKICA) or buy a paper ticket at Yui Rail stations; a single monorail ride is about ¥230-370 by distance, and the 1-day and 2-day passes are good value. Buses take cash, OKICA, and now most national IC cards.
transit.hours: The Yui Rail monorail runs roughly 6 AM to midnight; city buses run daytime into the evening with sparser night service, so taxis fill late-night trips.
transit.note: The Yui Rail monorail is the prefecture's only train - a single elevated line running from Naha Airport through Kokusai-dori and Omoromachi up to Shuri and Tedako-Uranishi. Buses cover everywhere else, but to explore the wider island most visitors rent a car.

ferry: Ferries to the Kerama Islands and Kagoshima

food.name: Okinawa soba
food.desc: Chewy wheat noodles in a clear pork-and-bonito broth, topped with stewed pork belly or soft-stewed rib, pickled ginger and green onion.

places.name: Su-manume
places.note: Renovated wooden house serving additive-free broth and bone-in pork; a Naha soba benchmark.

places.name: Ryukyu Soba Ashibiuna
places.note: Long-running favourite near Shuri Castle with a garden courtyard and classic soki soba.

places.name: Shuri Soba
places.note: Handmade noodles and simple pork broth; queues form well before lunch on weekends.

food.name: Goya champuru
food.desc: Okinawa's signature stir-fry of bitter melon with firm island tofu, egg and pork or spam; bracingly bitter and eaten year-round.

places.name: Yunangii
places.note: Home-style Okinawan kitchen off Kokusai-dori; champuru cooked the way families make it.

places.name: Urizun
places.note: Institution since 1972 for Ryukyu home cooking; reliable champuru and a huge awamori list.

places.name: Dachibin
places.note: Izakaya in an old Okinawan house with live sanshin music alongside the stir-fries.

food.name: Rafute
food.desc: Pork belly simmered for hours in awamori, soy and brown sugar until the fat turns to jelly; a Ryukyu court dish now on every izakaya menu.

places.name: Yunangii
places.note: Rafute is the house speciality, braised until it collapses under chopsticks.

places.name: Urizun
places.note: Classic Ryukyu-cuisine spread; order rafute with the tofu-yo fermented tofu.

places.name: Dachibin
places.note: Generous portions and awamori pairings in a lively converted-house setting.

food.name: Taco rice
food.desc: Post-war Okinawan invention: seasoned taco beef, lettuce, tomato and cheese piled over rice, often with salsa on the side.

places.name: THE TACORICE HOUSE
places.note: Dedicated taco-rice specialist in central Naha with several sauce and topping options.

places.name: Amigo Tacos
places.note: Small counter shop praised for its house salsa and quick, friendly service.

places.name: Kokusai-dori Yataimura
places.note: Food-stall village where several stalls serve taco rice late into the evening.

food.name: Sata andagi
food.desc: Okinawan doughnut balls with a craggy split top, crisp outside and cakey within; sold warm by the bag at markets and festivals.

places.name: Makishi Public Market
places.note: Ground-floor stalls fry them through the day; buy a bag while browsing the fish counters.

places.name: Kokusai-dori confectioners
places.note: Several sweet shops along the strip sell brown-sugar and purple-sweet-potato versions.

places.name: Ryubo depachika
places.note: Department-store food hall with boxed sata andagi from established Okinawan makers.

food.name: Umibudo and Agu pork
food.desc: Sea grapes that pop like caviar, served with ponzu, plus shabu-shabu or grilled cuts of sweet native Agu pork.

places.name: Makishi Public Market
places.note: Buy umibudo downstairs and have upstairs cooks prepare your fish and pork.

places.name: Urizun
places.note: Dependable place to try umibudo alongside the rest of the Ryukyu repertoire.

places.name: Yunangii
places.note: Small menu of island produce including sea grapes and local pork dishes.

food.name: Awamori
food.desc: Okinawa's indigenous distilled spirit made from long-grain rice and black koji; drunk on the rocks or cut with water, aged versions called kusu.

places.name: Urizun
places.note: Famous cellar of aged kusu from distilleries across the islands; tasting flights available.

places.name: Dachibin
places.note: Wide awamori range poured alongside sanshin performances most nights.

places.name: Kokusai-dori Yataimura
places.note: Stall village where you can hop between bars sampling different island distilleries.

food.name: Shikuwasa juice
food.desc: Tart green citrus native to northern Okinawa, pressed into a sharp cordial or juice and drunk chilled; also splashed over soba and grilled fish.

places.name: Makishi Public Market
places.note: Fruit stalls sell fresh-pressed shikuwasa and bottled cordial to take home.

places.name: Kokusai-dori juice stands
places.note: Walk-up stands squeeze shikuwasa and pineapple to order along the main strip.

places.name: Ryubo depachika
places.note: Reliable selection of island-made shikuwasa drinks and vinegars under one roof.

landmarks: Shuri Castle
The reconstructed royal Ryukyu Kingdom castle, with its vivid vermillion walls and distinctive Ryukyuan-Chinese architecture, is Okinawa's premier UNESCO World Heritage icon.
Shureimon Gate
This ornate crimson gate, once featured on Japan's 2,000-yen banknote, is the iconic photo-op entrance to the Shuri Castle grounds.
Kankaimon Gate
The imposing main gate of Shuri Castle, flanked by stone dragon-guardian pillars, is a striking symbol of Ryukyuan royal power.
Kokusai-dōri (International Street)
Naha's vibrant 1.6-kilometer main thoroughfare buzzes with shops, street food, and neon energy, capturing the lively spirit of modern Okinawa.
Naminoue Shrine
Perched dramatically on a seaside cliff above Naminoue Beach, this Okinawan shrine offers one of Naha's most striking combinations of red torii, sea, and sky.
Tsuboya Pottery District
A charming cobblestone quarter lined with centuries-old kilns and pottery shops selling traditional Okinawan Yachimun ware, ideal for atmospheric photography.
Fukushuen Garden
An elaborate Chinese-style garden built to honor Naha's sister-city ties with Fuzhou, featuring ornate pavilions, bridges, and ponds amid dramatic limestone rockwork.
Makishi Public Market
Naha's famous covered market bursts with colorful tropical fish, seafood, and local produce, offering an unforgettable sensory slice of Okinawan daily life.
Shikinaen Garden
This exquisite former royal Ryukyuan garden retreat blends Chinese and Japanese landscaping around a tranquil pond, making it a serene UNESCO-listed photo destination.
Okinawa Prefectural Museum & Art Museum
A striking modern museum shaped to evoke a Ryukyuan gusuku fortress, showcasing Okinawa's natural history, culture, and art in a bold architectural statement.

train.note: Japan has no international trains, and Okinawa has no conventional railway or JR line at all - the wartime Okinawa Prefectural Railway was never rebuilt. The only rail is the Yui Rail monorail, 19 stations from Naha Airport through Asahibashi, Kokusai-dori and Shuri to Tedako-Uranishi in Urasoe. It is pay-as-you-go with paper tickets or OKICA/Suica cards, so no reservation is needed, and it does not connect to any other island or to the mainland. A Japan Rail Pass is worthless here.

bus.note: There are no international buses from Japan, and no bus reaches Okinawa from the mainland. The Naha Bus Terminal at Asahibashi, on the monorail and rebuilt as part of the Ryubo/OPA complex, is the hub for the island-wide network run by Okinawa Bus, Ryukyu Bus Kotsu, Naha Bus and Toyo Bus, including the express highway buses up the Okinawa Expressway to Nago and the Churaumi Aquarium (about 2-3 hours). Buy tickets on board or with an IC card; airport limousine buses to the resort areas are booked separately. Services are sparse outside the main corridor, so many visitors rent a car.

ferry.note: Naha is Okinawa's ferry hub, and the two ports do different jobs: Tomari Port (Tomarin), a short walk from Miebashi monorail station, handles the island boats, while Naha Port takes the long-distance ships. Fast ferries reach the Kerama Islands - Tokashiki, Zamami and Aka - in 35-70 minutes and are prized for diving; they fill up in summer and tickets are usually issued only on the day of travel, so reserve online and arrive 30 minutes early. A'LINE and Marix Line alternate a roughly 25-hour overnight voyage to Kagoshima on mainland Kyushu via the Amami islands, and A'LINE also runs cargo ships to Tokyo, Kobe/Osaka and Kitakyushu with limited or no passenger capacity. There are no scheduled international passenger ferries from Okinawa, and all sailings are cancelled in typhoons, which are frequent from July to October.

half.name: Shurijo Castle Park
half.blurb: The reconstructed hilltop palace of the Ryukyu Kingdom and its UNESCO-listed sacred sites, a short monorail ride from downtown.

half.name: Senagajima Island
half.blurb: A tiny causeway-linked island by the airport with the Umikaji Terrace shops and cafes, and planes roaring low overhead.

half.name: Okinawa World & Gyokusendo Cave
half.blurb: A culture theme park built over a vast limestone cavern, with Eisa drumming and a habu snake show in the island's south.

full.name: Churaumi Aquarium & Motobu
full.blurb: One of the world's great aquariums, with whale sharks and manta rays, on the scenic northern Motobu Peninsula (~2 hr).

full.name: Kerama Islands (Zamami / Tokashiki)
full.blurb: A fast ferry from Tomari Port reaches some of Japan's clearest water and best snorkeling and diving beaches.

full.name: Cape Manzamo & the Onna Coast
full.blurb: The elephant-trunk sea cliff and the resort beaches of the central west coast, a scenic drive up Route 58.
